content: Morphea, also known as localized scleroderma, is an immune-mediated condition characterized by excessive collagen production and deposition in the skin and underlying connective tissues, leading to areas of skin hardening. The clinical presentation of morphea varies depending on the subtype and stage of the disease. Currently, there is no established consensus on the most effective treatment strategies for this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various treatments for individuals diagnosed with any form of morphea. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed topical, intralesional, or systemic therapies, either alone or in combination, in patients clinically diagnosed with morphea. Comparisons were made against placebo, no intervention, other treatments, or different doses or durations of the same treatment. The primary outcomes of interest were global improvement in disease activity or damage, as assessed by medical practitioners or participants, and the occurrence of adverse effects. Secondary outcomes included specific improvements in disease activity and damage. The quality of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 14 RCTs involving 429 participants aged 3 to 76 years were included in the review. The participants included both children and adults, with a majority being female. Most participants had circumscribed morphea, followed by linear scleroderma. The studies were conducted in various settings, including dermatology centers, pediatric rheumatology and dermatology centers, and university hospitals. The trials evaluated a range of treatments, including topical, intralesional, and systemic therapies, with study durations ranging from seven weeks to 15 months. Due to the heterogeneity of the interventions and outcomes, no meta-analyses were performed. One RCT involving 70 juvenile participants with active morphea (linear scleroderma, generalized morphea, or mixed morphea) compared oral methotrexate (15 mg/m², maximum 20 mg, once weekly for 12 months or until disease flare) plus oral prednisone (1 mg/kg daily, maximum 50 mg, for three months, followed by a tapering dose) to placebo plus oral prednisone. The results suggested that oral methotrexate combined with prednisone may lead to greater global improvement in disease activity or damage compared to placebo plus prednisone (risk ratio [RR] 2.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.20 to 4.45; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] = 3). However, data were not available for individual morphea subtypes. Adverse events were reported in both groups, with methotrexate-associated side effects including alopecia, nausea, headache, fatigue, and hepatotoxicity. Prednisone-related adverse effects, observed in both groups, included weight gain (greater than 5% of body weight) and striae rubrae. There may be little or no difference in the number of participants experiencing at least one adverse event between the methotrexate and placebo groups (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.75 to 2.04). Another RCT compared three phototherapy regimens in children and adults with active morphea (circumscribed morphea, linear scleroderma, generalized morphea, or mixed morphea): medium-dose UVA-1 (50 J/cm²), low-dose UVA-1 (20 J/cm²), and narrowband UVB. Participants received phototherapy five times a week for eight weeks. The results indicated that there may be little or no difference in global improvement of disease activity or damage between the three treatments, as measured by the modified skin score. Safety data from the same trial suggested that UVA-1 phototherapy may cause mild tanning more frequently than narrowband UVB. However, there was no difference in the incidence of mild tanning between mediumand low-dose UVA-1 phototherapy. Transient erythema was reported in three participants treated with narrowband UVB but not in those receiving UVA-1 phototherapy. The authors concluded that oral methotrexate combined with oral prednisone may improve disease activity or damage in juvenile active morphea compared to placebo plus prednisone, but there may be a slightly increased risk of experiencing at least one adverse event. When comparing medium-dose UVA-1, low-dose UVA-1, and narrowband UVB phototherapy in children and adults with active morphea, there may be little or no difference in global improvement of disease activity or damage. However, UVA-1 phototherapy may cause more mild tanning than narrowband UVB, with no difference between mediumand low-dose UVA-1. These findings are based on low-quality evidence, with limitations including a high risk of bias, small sample sizes, and imprecise results. The authors recommend conducting multicenter RCTs with larger sample sizes and validated tools to assess treatment responses across different morphea subtypes and age groups.
